messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At sixty-seven, Tane moved through his Honolulu design studio with the careful, measured steps of a man mapping an exit before he entered a room. Years ago, while coordinating a remote infrastructure project in the Levant, he had been taken by armed men and held in a windowless concrete cell for eleven days. The captivity had ended only when a diplomatic corridor opened, but the silence that followed was far louder than the shouts that had preceded it. In that cell, captors had paced the floor, their voices a relentless wall of shouting in Arabic that pierced his sleep long after the bars were gone. He remembered the rough concrete against his spine, the terrifying weight of feeling emotionally vulnerable with no way to shield himself, and the way his body would react to danger before his mind could process the threat. In the months that followed, the memory of that cell never softened. When he tried to recount the ordeal to his late wife, he would lose the thread mid-sentence, unable to explain clearly what had transpired. When the recollection finally broke through, it arrived as an emotionless recall, as though the suffering belonged to a stranger, yet it was always accompanied by the same auditory recall of those distant voices echoing in his skull. The shame and horror of being held against his will began to pool in his gut, and those negative emotions quickly hardened into a permanent state of alert. As the dread deepened, it sharpened his awareness of danger, making every unfamiliar sound feel like a precursor to capture. When the auditory recall spiked, the weight of those negative emotions grew, and the fear would tighten his throat until he could no longer piece together what had actually happened. The triggers that now governed his days were unrelenting. A dropped book would startle him into a sudden intrusive memory of the cell, and the feeling of vulnerability would wash over him so completely that his body reacted to danger before he had even had time to think. He learned to scan every room for the nearest structural column, needing his back to a wall where he could see the entire space before his heart would steady. Those triggers quickly forged a rigid set of coping habits; every time the Arabic whispers seemed to bleed into a foreign accent on the radio, or when a sudden noise pierced his quiet evenings, he would retreat into his studio’s guest room to rehearse conversations, running through polite professional scripts until the panic subsided. The constant fear also pushed him to avoid enclosed spaces altogether, so he began declining site visits, letting the heavy steel doors of client basements and windowless storage rooms feel like traps he simply would not enter. Over time, these avoidance patterns carved deeper channels in his mind. By rehearsing conversations and avoiding work or study, he starved the memories of any chance to be integrated; the unprocessed fragments only grew more detached, leaving him with emotionless recall whenever he tried to reflect on his past. The very strategies meant to protect him now fed the threat system, keeping his nervous system locked in a state of negative emotions and hyperalertness. He found himself avoiding work or study as the design firm’s quarterly reviews approached, telling himself he needed more time to rest, when in truth the thought of sitting in a small conference room with colleagues felt unbearable. Each day he stayed away from the drafting tables, the fear of being found vulnerable in an exposed space compounded, and the negative emotions would surface as a quiet, relentless guilt that he was shrinking from his own career. Now, at sixty-seven, Tane sits on the edge of his living room sofa, his shoulders angled toward the nearest bookshelf, listening to the rain drum against the windows. The weight of eleven years has settled into his posture; he has come to believe that stepping into his studio again means risking the old helplessness, and that speaking the words out loud will only invite the shame back into the room. What frightened him most was the realization that his own silence was slowly eroding the life he had worked to rebuild. He finally called the community mental health center not because the shouting has stopped, but because he is desperate to remember who he was before the captivity, and he is hoping, for the first time, that someone might help him untangle the thread before it slips away entirely.
